title: Were Roman Soldiers Really Paid in Salt?

beats.say: You've probably heard this one. The word salary comes from salt, because Roman soldiers were paid in salt. It's in quiz books, school lessons and countless websites. There's just one problem. There's no good evidence it's true.
Today's lesson is a detective story about a word. Where it came from, how a myth grew around it, and what it teaches us about checking the stories we hear about money.
Lesson one. The word.
Let's start with what is true. The English word salary comes from the Latin word salarium. And salarium is connected to sal, the Latin word for salt. So far, so good.
In Roman times, salarium was used for a payment or allowance, often to officials. But here's the catch. Nobody in ancient times actually explained why the word was linked to salt.

vis.text: Nobody in ancient times explained the link.

beats.say: Lesson two. How soldiers were really paid.

So how were Roman soldiers paid? Mainly in coins. Their basic pay was called stipendium, and it was paid in money, mostly silver coins called denarii. Deductions were taken for food, clothing and equipment.
Historians have records of Roman military pay, including deductions for things like food and boots. Salt doesn't appear as a form of wages.

A Roman legionary's pay was a big deal. It was paid a few times a year, and much of it was kept back to cover costs. Soldiers also received bonuses, called donatives, from emperors trying to keep the army loyal.
Lesson three. Where the myth came from.
Part of the myth comes from a passage by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, in his huge encyclopedia, Natural History. He wrote at length about salt, and praised how important it was.

vis.sub: Wrote about salt in Natural History

beats.say: In that passage, Pliny mentions salt and the word salarium near each other. But he doesn't clearly say soldiers were paid in salt. Later writers read more into it than he actually said.

vis.text: Later writers read too much into it.

beats.say: The story really took off much later. Dictionaries in the eighteen hundreds added the idea that salt had been part of Roman soldiers' pay. Once it was in respected reference books, it spread everywhere.
In recent years, scholars have pushed back. The dictionary publisher Merriam-Webster says the idea of soldiers being paid in salt money has no basis in ancient sources.

vis.text: Has no basis in ancient sources.

beats.say: Lesson four. So why salt?
If the soldiers weren't paid in salt, why is salarium linked to salt at all? Honestly, nobody knows for sure. There are a few theories.

vis.title: Possible explanations
items: Linked to guards on salt roads

beats.say: Some suggest it could have started as an allowance to buy salt, or been connected to the famous salt road into Rome, the Via Salaria. But these are educated guesses, not proven facts.
Here's another surprise. Some people say soldier comes from salt too. It doesn't. It comes from solidus, a Roman gold coin. So soldiers were named after money, just not salt.
Lesson five. Salt really was valuable.

The myth survives partly because salt really was important in the ancient world. Before fridges, salt was one of the main ways to preserve meat and fish. People and animals needed it. And it was heavily traded and taxed.

And salt really has been used as money, just not by Roman soldiers. In parts of Ethiopia, blocks of salt were used as currency for centuries. In parts of China and Tibet, salt was used in trade and as money too.

right.title: Elsewhere
lines: Salt money in China and Tibet

beats.say: So the idea of salt as money isn't crazy. It's just been attached to the wrong people.

vis.text: Salt money was real. Just not for Romans.

beats.say: Even the phrase worth his salt, meaning someone who deserves their pay, is often linked to the Roman story. But that phrase only appears much later, in the eighteen hundreds.
Lesson six. Why this matters.
Why spend five minutes on a word? Because the salt story is a perfect example of how a neat, satisfying explanation can spread for centuries without anyone checking the original sources.
Money is full of stories like this. Investment tips, rules of thumb, things everyone just knows. The habit of asking where's the evidence is one of the most valuable money skills you can have.
So next time someone tells you salary comes from Roman soldiers being paid in salt, you can tell them the word really does come from salt. But the soldiers? They were paid in silver.

vis.text: The word, yes. The soldiers, no.

beats.say: Lesson over. Subscribe for more surprising stories from the history of money, and tell me in the comments which money myth I should check next.
